content: Interleukin-2 receptor antagonists (IL2Ra) are utilized as induction therapy to prevent acute rejection in kidney transplant recipients. Since their introduction, the use of IL2Ra has steadily increased, though the proportion of new transplant recipients receiving IL2Ra varies globally. For instance, in 2007, 27% of new kidney transplant recipients in the United States received IL2Ra, compared to 70% in Australasia. The objective of this analysis was to systematically evaluate the effects of IL2Ra when used in addition to standard therapy or as an alternative to other immunosuppressive induction strategies. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Renal Group’s specialized register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing IL2Ra to placebo, no treatment, other IL2Ra, or other antibody therapies were included. Data extraction and analysis were performed independently by two authors, with discrepancies resolved through discussion. Dichotomous outcomes were reported as relative risk (RR), and continuous outcomes were expressed as mean difference (MD), both with 95% confidence intervals (CI). A total of 71 studies, encompassing 306 reports and 10,520 participants, were included in the analysis. When IL2Ra was compared to placebo (32 studies, 5,854 patients), the risk of graft loss, including death with a functioning graft, was reduced by 25% at six months (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.98) and one year (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.90), though this benefit was not observed beyond one year. At one year, biopsy-proven acute rejection was reduced by 28% (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.81), and the incidence of cytomegalovirus (CMV) disease decreased by 19% (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.97). Additionally, there was a 64% reduction in early malignancy within six months (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.86), and serum creatinine levels were lower (MD -8.18 µmol/L, 95% CI -14.28 to -2.09). However, these differences were not sustained over time. When IL2Ra was compared to antithymocyte globulin (ATG) (18 studies, 1,844 participants), there was no significant difference in graft loss at any time point or in clinically diagnosed acute rejection. However, ATG demonstrated a benefit over IL2Ra for biopsy-proven acute rejection at one year (RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.67). This benefit came at the cost of a 75% increase in malignancy (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.87) and a 32% increase in CMV disease (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.93). Serum creatinine levels were significantly lower in IL2Ra-treated patients at six months (MD -11.20 µmol/L, 95% CI -19.94 to -2.09). Patients receiving ATG experienced significantly more adverse effects, including fever, cytokine release syndrome, and leukopenia, though thrombocytopenia was not observed. There were no significant differences in outcomes based on the use of cyclosporine or tacrolimus, azathioprine or mycophenolate, or the baseline risk of acute rejection in the study populations. Additionally, no differences were observed between equine and rabbit ATG. The authors concluded that, given a 38% risk of rejection, nine kidney transplant recipients would need to be treated with IL2Ra to prevent one case of rejection, 42 to prevent one case of graft loss, and 38 to prevent one case of CMV disease within the first year post-transplantation. Compared to ATG, IL2Ra may prevent CMV disease in 16 recipients and malignancy in 58 recipients for every one case prevented. There were no apparent differences in efficacy between the two IL2Ra agents, basiliximab and daclizumab. Overall, IL2Ra was found to be as effective as other antibody therapies, with significantly fewer side effects.
